narratives.narrative: The verse reads 'prepare' (sense 101) as a volition (type 102): an act the will orders, not a feeling that simply arrives. No prior source is recorded (103 absent) - the passage does not say what stirs the impulse; it shows the posture already resolved. The operation (106) is that at dawn the self lays out its prayer like a sacrifice and then keeps watch - disciplined expectancy - and its target (107) is expectant-waiting: the whole movement bends toward an answer not yet given. The bearer (105) is the psalmist, and the two beats are welded by a coupling (112) of prepare-and-watch, so the ordering and the watching are one motion, not two. No organ seats this (104 none): waiting here is a whole-self stance, not lodged in heart or eyes. Manner is unmarked (108 none), and intensity, specifier, and effect are all unrecorded (109/110/111 absent) - the verse grades no degree, adds no qualifier, and names no result inside itself; the watching is left open-ended, its outcome deferred. Nothing is forbidden (113 absent). The discovery note (114) confirms the reading: prayer set out, then alert waiting. It stands as a characteristic of the inner being (role 115) whose locus is the interior's own state (116) - the self disciplining itself toward God, who is the one watched for, not the actor here.
narratives.story: At first light the psalmist deliberately sets his prayer before God, laying it out as carefully as an offering, and then stays awake and alert for a reply. This is a chosen discipline, not a mood that washes over him: he readies himself and then watches, and the two acts are really one steady posture of expectation. The psalm does not say what first moved him to it, nor does it locate the waiting in any one part of him - it is his whole self leaning forward. It also does not tell us how intensely he waits or what finally comes of it; the watching is simply left open, its answer still ahead. What we see is a person schooling himself each morning to wait on God.

narratives.narrative: The sense (101) is that the poor's hope shall not perish, read as affect (type 102) - a felt orientation, not a deliberate act. Its bearer (105) is the poor and needy, and the operation (106) is that the needy are not forever forgotten nor their hope finally destroyed: hope that outlasts neglect, targeted (107) at enduring-hope. The coupling (112) hope-not-perish binds the interior movement to its own durability - the point of the reading is that this hope survives. No source is recorded (103 absent): the psalm does not trace where the poor's hope comes from, only that it holds. No seat locates it (104 none) - it is not an organ's act but the whole condition of the lowly. Manner is unmarked (108 none); intensity, specifier, and effect are unrecorded (109/110/111 absent) - no degree, no qualifier, and, tellingly, no in-verse outcome beyond the promise that it will not perish. Nothing is prohibited (113 absent). The discovery (114) underlines the finding: the interior of the poor holds a hope the psalm insists is durable, not finally disappointed. Role is characteristic (115); locus is the interior's own state (116). The lens stays on the inner life of the powerless - God is the arena their hope reaches toward, but the claim is about what endures inside them.
narratives.story: The psalm makes a quiet but stubborn claim: the hope carried by the poor and forgotten will not be crushed out of them. However long they are overlooked, that inner expectation survives. The psalm does not explain where such hope comes from or pin it to any single feeling; it simply insists the hope lasts. It does not measure how strong it is or spell out how it is finally rewarded within the verse - only that it will not perish. The focus stays on the durable inner life of people the world ignores.
narratives.variation_note: This reading of tiqvah is the enduring hope of the poor as a durable communal condition, whereas the same word at Psa 62:5 is the psalmist commanding his own soul and at Psa 71:5 is God himself named as a lifelong personal hope; here the bearer is a class (the needy) and the accent falls on hope surviving neglect rather than on its object.

narratives.narrative: 'Dwell' (sense 101) is read as affect (type 102) - the settled feeling of belonging rather than a willed act. The bearer (105) is the psalmist, and the operation (106) is that the self will dwell in the house of the LORD forever: a permanent hope of God's presence, targeted (107) at settled-hope. The coupling (112) dwell-forever fuses the movement to its own permanence - the finding is the unbrokenness. No source is recorded (103 absent): the psalm does not derive this rest from a prior cause; it arrives as the whole psalm's landing point. No seat locates it (104 none) - dwelling is not an organ's operation but the whole self's condition. Manner is unmarked (108 none); intensity, specifier, and effect are unrecorded (109/110/111 absent) - no degree, no qualifier, no separately named result; the permanence itself is the outcome. Nothing is prohibited (113 absent). The discovery (114) reads it as the psalm's resolution: the interior's final rest is unbroken nearness to God. Role is characteristic (115); its locus is the interior's own state (116) - the self at rest, with God as the home it rests in.
narratives.story: The psalm ends by settling: the writer knows he will live in God's house forever. This is not a plan he is working toward but a deep, restful certainty of belonging that has no end. The psalm does not argue for it or trace where it came from - it simply lands there, as the place the whole song has been heading. It gives no measure of the feeling and names no further result, because the permanence is the point. What we are left with is a person completely at home, and unbrokenly so, near God.

narratives.narrative: Here 'wait' (qavah, sense 101) is affect (type 102) - a felt trust generalised into patience. Its bearer (105) is those who wait, and the operation (106) is that none who wait for God are put to shame while the wantonly treacherous are: waiting as the vindicated posture, targeted (107) simply at waiting itself. The coupling (112) wait-not-shamed ties the inner posture to its promised outcome of non-disappointment. No source is recorded (103 absent) - the psalm does not say what generates the waiting, only that it will be honoured. No seat locates it (104 none): it is a whole-self stance, not an organ's act. Manner is unmarked (108 none); intensity, specifier, and effect are unrecorded (109/110/111 absent) - no degree, no qualifier, and the outcome, though promised (not shamed), is not spelled out as a separate in-verse effect. Nothing is prohibited (113 absent). The discovery (114) reads it as trust widened into patient waiting, promised it will not be disappointed. Role is characteristic (115); locus is the interior's own state (116) - the waiting self, with God as the one waited on.
narratives.story: The psalm draws a line between two kinds of people: those who wait on God, and those who betray without cause. The ones who wait, it promises, will never be humiliated for it. This is trust stretched out into patience - a settled inner leaning on God that is bound to be honoured rather than let down. The psalm does not say what first produces such waiting or how strong it must be; it simply guarantees the waiter will not be put to shame. The whole weight rests on the quiet confidence of the one who waits.
narratives.variation_note: This first qavah reading is general - a class of 'those who wait' promised vindication - and impersonal, distinct from Psa 25:5 immediately after, where the same verb becomes the psalmist's own unremitting, all-day waiting. Here waiting is a category promised safety; there it is a personal, sustained act.

narratives.narrative: 'Wait' (qavah, sense 101) is affect (type 102), but now personal: the self waits for God all day long while asking to be led in his truth. The bearer (105) is the psalmist, the operation (106) is sustained, whole-day hope, and the target (107) is sustained-waiting - the accent falls on duration. The coupling (112) wait-all-day binds the inner posture to the unbroken span of a day. No source is recorded (103 absent); no seat locates it (104 none) - it is the whole self, not an organ, that waits. Manner is unmarked (108 none); intensity, specifier, and effect are unrecorded (109/110/111 absent) - the verse grades no degree and names no separate result, though 'all the day long' functions within the operation itself as its temporal reach. Nothing is prohibited (113 absent). The discovery (114) marks it as the personal, unremitting waiting that fills the whole day, expressly distinct from v3. Role is characteristic (115); locus is the interior's own state (116) - the self held in expectancy toward God through every hour.
narratives.story: Now the waiting becomes personal and unbroken: the psalmist tells God he waits for him all day long, and in the same breath asks to be taught and led in the truth. This is not a passing glance upward but a whole day spent leaning on God. The psalm does not say what sparked it or how fiercely it burns; it simply stretches the waiting across every hour. The picture is of a person whose entire day is coloured by expectation toward God.
narratives.variation_note: Set against v3's general promise to 'those who wait', this reading is the psalmist's own first-person waiting, and its distinctive mark is duration - 'all the day long' - making it sustained personal expectancy rather than a category being reassured.

narratives.narrative: Here 'wait' (qavah, sense 101) shifts to volition (type 102): the self commands itself to wait. The bearer (105) is the psalmist, the operation (106) is the interior exhorting itself (and others) to wait for the LORD, be strong, and let the heart take courage - self-command to patient courage - with the target (107) being self-exhortation. The coupling (112) wait-and-courage welds waiting to the summoning of strength: waiting is not passive here but demands mustered courage. No source is recorded (103 absent); no seat locates the act (104 none), even though the verse names the heart as what must take courage - the waiting itself is not organ-seated. Manner is unmarked (108 none); intensity, specifier, and effect are unrecorded (109/110/111 absent) - no degree graded, no result named. Nothing is prohibited (113 absent). The discovery (114) reads it as the interior addressing itself, commanding the patience and courage it needs to keep waiting. Role is characteristic (115); locus is the interior's own state (116) - the self turning on itself to hold its ground toward God.
narratives.story: This time waiting takes the form of an order the psalmist gives himself: wait for the LORD, be strong, let your heart be brave, and wait again. Waiting here is anything but limp - it takes courage, and he has to rally himself to it. The psalm does not say what prompted the self-talk or how hard the struggle is; it simply shows a person bracing his own inner life to keep waiting. It is the sound of someone stiffening his resolve to stay hopeful when it would be easier to give up.
narratives.variation_note: Unlike the affect-readings at Psa 25, this qavah is volitional - the self commanding itself. Its distinctive is that waiting is coupled to courage and self-exhortation: not a promised outcome or a sustained mood but an act of will the interior musters against its own faltering.

narratives.narrative: 'Hope' (yachal, sense 101) is affect (type 102): a forward-leaning trust. The bearer (105) is those who hope, and the operation (106) is that the LORD's eye rests on those who hope in his steadfast love - hope leaning on covenant love as the ground of God's regard - with the target (107) simply hope. The coupling (112) hope-in-chesed anchors the interior movement to God's steadfast love as its resting-place. No source is recorded (103 absent): the psalm does not derive the hope from a prior cause, presenting it as the disposition God looks upon. No seat locates it (104 none) - not an organ's act but a whole-self stance. Manner is unmarked (108 none); intensity, specifier, and effect are unrecorded (109/110/111 absent) - no degree, no qualifier, and the effect (God's regarding eye) is narrated as operation rather than logged as a separate effect row. Nothing is prohibited (113 absent). The discovery (114) distinguishes this from fear: it is forward-leaning trust in God's love, the expectancy that draws his eye alongside reverence. Role is characteristic (115); locus is the interior's own state (116) - the hoping self, with God's love as the arena it leans into.
narratives.story: Those who set their hope on God's faithful love are the very people God keeps his eye on. Hope here is a leaning-forward of the heart, resting its whole weight on God's steady, covenant love. The psalm does not explain how the hope began or measure its strength; it simply says this kind of hope is what draws God's attention. Where fear looks up in awe, this hope leans forward in expectation - and it is met by God's watching care.
narratives.variation_note: Within the same passage this reading is the general company of 'those who hope', the disposition God's eye rests on, whereas its neighbour at v22 is the community's own present hope offered as the ground of a closing plea. Here hope is the watched-for posture; there it is the leverage of a prayer.

narratives.narrative: 'Hope' (yachal, sense 101) is again affect (type 102), but now first-person and communal: the self asks God's steadfast love to rest upon it, even as it hopes in him. The bearer (105) is the community, the operation (106) makes present hope the ground of the closing plea, and the target (107) is present-hope. The coupling (112) as-we-hope ties the petition to the interior's active hoping - the hope is offered as the reason the request should be granted. No source is recorded (103 absent); no seat locates it (104 none) - a whole-self, whole-community stance. Manner is unmarked (108 none); intensity, specifier, and effect are unrecorded (109/110/111 absent) - no degree, no qualifier, no separately named result beyond the plea itself. Nothing is prohibited (113 absent). The discovery (114) marks it as distinct from v18's general hopers: this is the community's own present hope, offered as the reason for the plea. Role is characteristic (115); locus is the interior's own state (116) - the hoping community, with God's love as what it reaches for.
narratives.story: The psalm ends with a request: let your faithful love rest on us, just as we are hoping in you. Here the community turns its own hope into the grounds of its prayer - because we hope, let your love come. It is a present, active leaning on God, offered up as the very reason God should answer. The psalm does not say how the hope arose or how strong it is; it simply lays that hope before God as the basis for asking.
narratives.variation_note: Distinct from v18's general 'those who hope' whom God watches, this reading is the worshippers' own first-person hope in the moment, used as the lever of the closing petition - hope not described from outside but voiced from within as the ground of a plea.

narratives.narrative: 'Wait' (chul, sense 101: be still and wait patiently) is volition (type 102) - a commanded stilling. The bearer (105) is the hearer, and the operation (106) is that the self is told to be still before the LORD and wait patiently, not fretting over the one who prospers - quiet, patient stillness - targeted (107) at stillness. The coupling (112) be-still-and-wait binds waiting to inner quiet: the movement is the ceasing of agitation. No source is recorded (103 absent); no seat locates it (104 none) - the stilling is a whole-self posture, not an organ's act. Manner is unmarked (108 none); intensity, specifier, and effect are unrecorded (109/110/111 absent) - no degree graded, no result named. Nothing is prohibited within this row (113 absent), though the surrounding verse forbids fretting - here that negative is folded into the operation rather than logged as a prohibition. The discovery (114) reads it as an inner quiet: the interior stops agitating and holds still before God. Role is characteristic (115); locus is the interior's own state (116) - the self quieted, with the prospering wrongdoer as the provocation it must not answer with anxiety.
narratives.story: The instruction is to go quiet: be still before God and wait for him patiently, and stop working yourself up over people who seem to get away with everything. Waiting here means calming down - deliberately refusing to let the success of the wicked stir you into anxiety. The psalm does not say where the calm comes from or how hard it is to hold; it simply commands the inner life to settle. It is the picture of a restless heart being told to be quiet and trust.

narratives.narrative: 'Wait' (qavah, sense 101) here is volition (type 102) and active: the self is told to wait for the LORD and keep his way, and he will exalt it to inherit the land. The bearer (105) is the hearer, the operation (106) joins patient waiting to obedient keeping, and the target (107) is patient-obedience. The coupling (112) wait-and-keep-way is the key finding: waiting is fused to walking in God's way - not idle expectancy but expectancy that obeys while it waits. No source is recorded (103 absent); no seat locates it (104 none) - a whole-self stance. Manner is unmarked (108 none); intensity, specifier, and effect are unrecorded (109/110/111 absent) - no degree graded, and the promised exaltation is carried inside the operation rather than logged as a separate effect. Nothing is prohibited (113 absent). The discovery (114) marks it as distinct from v7's stillness: this waiting is active, coupled with keeping God's way. Role is characteristic (115); locus is the interior's own state (116) - the self both waiting and obeying, with God as the one who will act on both.
narratives.story: Wait for the LORD and keep to his path - do both, and he will lift you up to inherit the land. Waiting here is not sitting idle; it walks God's way while it waits. The two go together: expectation and obedience are one posture. The psalm does not spell out where such waiting comes from or how intense it must be, and it folds the promised reward into the command itself. The picture is of someone who keeps living rightly precisely because he is still waiting on God to act.
narratives.variation_note: Against the same psalm's earlier call to 'be still and wait patiently' (v7), this qavah is active rather than quiet: its distinctive is the coupling of waiting with keeping God's way, so patience here does work - it obeys - rather than merely holding still.

narratives.narrative: 'Wait' (yachal, sense 101) is affect (type 102): the sufferer's hope fixed on God's response. The bearer (105) is the psalmist, and the operation (106) is that for the LORD the self waits, for it is he who will answer - hope fixed on God's response - with the target (107) simply waiting. The coupling (112) wait-you-answer binds the interior waiting to the expected divine reply: the whole posture leans on God speaking. No source is recorded (103 absent); no seat locates it (104 none) - a whole-self stance. Manner is unmarked (108 none); intensity, specifier, and effect are unrecorded (109/110/111 absent) - no degree graded, no separate result logged. Nothing is prohibited (113 absent). The discovery (114) reads it as the turn from silence to hope: the interior stops defending itself and waits for God to speak. Role is characteristic (115); locus is the interior's own state (116) - the self, having gone silent before its accusers, now waiting on God alone to answer.
narratives.story: Surrounded by accusers and having chosen to stay silent, the psalmist turns his whole hope toward God: it is you I wait for, and you who will answer. Waiting here is the moment he stops defending himself and hands the response over to God. The psalm does not say how the hope began or how strong it is; it simply shows him leaning everything on God being the one to speak. It is the quiet pivot of a cornered man from self-defence to trust.
narratives.variation_note: This yachal is the waiting of a besieged, silent sufferer whose whole hope is that God will answer - distinct from Psa 69:3, where the same word describes hope strained to the point that the eyes fail from watching. Here waiting is a deliberate turn from self-defence to God; there it is expectation worn to exhaustion.

narratives.narrative: 'Wait' (qavah, sense 101) is affect (type 102): expectancy stripped down to its one object. The bearer (105) is the psalmist, and the operation (106) is that against the vanity of life the self asks for what it waits and answers that its hope is in the Lord alone - hope narrowed to God - with the target (107) narrowed-hope. The coupling (112) hope-in-you binds the interior movement to God as its sole remaining object. No source is recorded (103 absent); no seat locates it (104 none) - a whole-self stance. Manner is unmarked (108 none); intensity, specifier, and effect are unrecorded (109/110/111 absent) - no degree graded, no separate result. Nothing is prohibited (113 absent). The discovery (114) reads it as the collapse of every other hope into one: if all is breath, the interior fastens its whole expectancy on God. Role is characteristic (115); locus is the interior's own state (116) - the self, having seen life's futility, converging its whole hope onto God.
narratives.story: Having just called all of life fleeting and empty, the psalmist asks himself what he is even waiting for - and answers: my hope is in you. Every other thing he might have waited on has fallen away as vapour, and what remains is God alone. The psalm does not explain how the hope arose or measure it; it simply shows every lesser expectation collapsing into one. It is the sound of a disillusioned man discovering that God is the only thing left worth hoping in.
narratives.variation_note: Where other qavah readings promise or sustain waiting, this one is born of disillusion: its distinctive is that hope is narrowed - everything else exposed as breath - until God alone remains its object. Waiting here is what is left after every other hope is emptied out.

narratives.narrative: 'Wait' (qavah, sense 101) is affect (type 102), and here it is remembered as already answered: I waited patiently, and he heard my cry. The bearer (105) is the psalmist, the operation (106) is that the self waited patiently for the LORD, who inclined to it and heard its cry - patient waiting rewarded - with the target (107) patient-waiting. The coupling (112) waited-and-heard binds the interior patience to God's answering attention: this is the one reading where the waiting is narrated to its outcome. No source is recorded (103 absent); no seat locates it (104 none) - a whole-self stance. Manner is unmarked (108 none); intensity, specifier, and effect are unrecorded (109/110/111 absent) - even here the answer is carried inside the operation rather than logged as a separate effect row, and no degree is graded. Nothing is prohibited (113 absent). The discovery (114) reads it as sustained, quiet waiting that God bent down to answer: patience met by attention. Role is characteristic (115); locus is the interior's own state (116) - the self that waited, with God as the one who inclined and heard.
narratives.story: Looking back, the psalmist testifies: I waited and waited for the LORD, and he leaned down and heard my cry. Here the waiting is not left hanging - it is remembered as answered, patience that God actually bent down to meet. The psalm does not say how the waiting began or how long it stretched, only that it was quiet and sustained and that God responded. It is the grateful memory of a person whose patience was rewarded by being heard.
narratives.variation_note: Almost alone among these qavah readings, this one is retrospective and fulfilled: its distinctive is the coupling 'waited-and-heard' - patience narrated through to God's answer - rather than the open, unresolved waiting of the others, where the outcome is still ahead.

narratives.narrative: This yachal 'hope' (sense 101) is typed as action (102) rather than mere affect - the deliberate command to hope. Uniquely for this item the source is recorded (103): God his salvation, the object of hope, given as a span-pair - the hope has a named ground. The bearer (105) is the soul, self-commanded (a span-pair from the refrain), and the operation (106) is simply hope, targeted (107) at God. The coupling (112) is that the soul is commanded to it - a span-pair binding the act to the self it is addressed to. No seat locates it (104 none) - not organ-lodged. Manner is unmarked (108 none); intensity, specifier, and effect are unrecorded (109/110/111 absent) - no degree graded, no separate result. Nothing is prohibited (113 absent). The discovery (114) reads it as the reiterated refrain: the disciplined hope that answers recurring dejection, the psalm's closing counsel to the self. Role is characteristic (115); and its locus (116) is external:god - the hope oriented outward on God, its salvation. God is the arena; the inner-being movement is the downcast self ordering itself to hope.
narratives.story: For the third time in the psalm the writer turns and speaks to his own sinking soul: why are you cast down? Hope in God. This closing repetition is a discipline - each time despair rises, he answers it by commanding himself to hope, and he names what that hope rests on: God, his salvation. Hope here is a deliberate act the self orders, aimed squarely at God. It is a man refusing to let his own dejection have the last word, steering his whole inner life back toward the God he trusts to save him.
narratives.variation_note: This closing refrain (v11) and its twin at v5 both command the downcast soul to hope, and both name God as the object; the difference is placement and finality - v5 first answers the dejection midway, while v11 is the psalm's last word, the counsel that ends the debate. The reading is held distinct chiefly as the concluding instance.

narratives.narrative: This yachal 'hope' (sense 101) is action (type 102): the self-command to hope against dejection. The source is recorded (103): God his salvation, the object of hope, as a span-pair - the hope is grounded in God who saves. The bearer (105) is the soul, self-commanded (span-pair), the operation (106) is hope, targeted (107) at God, and the coupling (112) is that the soul is commanded to it (span-pair). No seat locates it (104 none). Manner is unmarked (108 none); intensity, specifier, and effect are unrecorded (109/110/111 absent) - no degree graded, no separate result. Nothing is prohibited (113 absent). The discovery (114) reads it as the deliberate turning of the downcast soul toward God, its salvation - the discipline of hope. Role is characteristic (115); locus (116) is external:god - the hope oriented outward on God. This same reading recurs verbatim at Psa 43:5, where the refrain repeats in the neighbouring psalm. The inner-being movement is the self dividing into speaker and soul, ordering the sunk part of itself to hope.
narratives.story: In the middle of his depression the psalmist does a striking thing: he talks to himself. Why are you so downcast? he asks his own soul - then commands it, hope in God, for I will praise him again. Hope is something he chooses and orders, not something he waits to feel, and it aims straight at God his rescuer. The very same words come back in the next psalm, showing this is a settled habit. It is the picture of a person split in two - one part collapsing, the other steadily pulling it back toward hope in God.
narratives.variation_note: This is the first occurrence of the refrain (v5), answering the dejection midway through the psalm, and it recurs identically at Psa 43:5; its object is God his salvation. It is held distinct from v11 mainly by position - the mid-psalm turn versus the closing counsel - the words and movement being the same.

narratives.narrative: 'Wait/hope' (qavah, sense 101: I will wait for your name) is action (type 102). The source is recorded (103): because God's name is good - a span-pair; the waiting is grounded not in circumstance but in God's character. The bearer (105) is the psalmist, the operation (106) is to wait/hope for, and the target (107) is your name (a span-pair) - God's revealed character, not merely his help. Uniquely, manner is recorded (108): in the presence of the godly - the waiting is voiced publicly, among the faithful. The coupling (112) pairs it with thanksgiving (span-pair): waiting welded to praise. No seat locates it (104 none). Intensity, specifier, and effect are unrecorded (109/110/111 absent) - no degree graded, no separate result. Nothing is prohibited (113 absent). The discovery (114) reads it as expectant hope in God's revealed character, grounded in who God is, voiced among the godly. Role is characteristic (115); locus (116) is external:god - oriented outward on God's name. The inner-being movement is a hope anchored in God's known goodness and confessed openly.
narratives.story: The psalm closes by turning waiting into worship: I will wait for your name, the writer says, because it is good - and he says it out loud among God's faithful people. His hope is not pinned to how things happen to turn out but to the kind of God he knows God to be. Waiting and thanksgiving run together here, and it is done in public, among the godly, not in private. It is a person confidently looking to God's good character, and glad to say so where others can hear.
narratives.variation_note: Among the qavah readings this one is distinctive on three counts: its ground is stated (God's name is good), its setting is named (before the godly), and it is fused to thanksgiving - waiting here is public, grounded, praising hope, rather than the private or unresolved waiting elsewhere.

narratives.narrative: This is qavah turned dark: 'wait/lie in wait' (sense 101: they waited for my life) is action (type 102), but the bearer (105) is the enemies. The operation (106) is to lie in wait for, and the target (107) is my life, nefesh (a span-pair) - the very seat of the psalmist's being. The coupling (112) pairs it with watching his steps (span-pair): patient surveillance welded to the ambush. No source is recorded (103 absent) - the psalm does not explain the malice, only its patient intent. No seat locates it (104 none); manner is unmarked (108 none); intensity, specifier, and effect are unrecorded (109/110/111 absent) - no degree graded, no separate result. Nothing is prohibited (113 absent). The discovery (114) is the finding to hold without flinching: the same verb that elsewhere names hope in God is here perverted into a hope for his death - patient malice, an expectant lurking. Role is characteristic (115); locus (116) is external:person - oriented on other people. Read with equal weight to the bright readings: the interior of the wicked also 'waits', and its expectancy is aimed at destroying a life.
narratives.story: The same word that everywhere else means hoping in God is here twisted into something sinister: the psalmist's enemies wait for his life, patiently watching his every move for the chance to strike. Their waiting is a kind of dark hope - not for God, but for his death. The psalm does not explain what drives them; it just shows the patient, expectant menace of it. It is a chilling reminder that the human capacity to wait and hope can be bent toward murder as easily as toward God.
narratives.variation_note: This qavah is the shadow-side of the family: bearer is the enemies, not a worshipper, and the target is the psalmist's life rather than God. Its distinctive - and the finding - is that the very verb of hope-in-God is here inverted into predatory, patient malice, waiting for a death.

narratives.narrative: 'Lie in wait/ambush' (arab, sense 101: they lie in wait for my life) is action (type 102), and like the qavah at Psa 56 its bearer (105) is the enemies. The operation (106) is to lie in wait, to ambush, and the target (107) is my life, nefesh (a span-pair). The coupling (112) pairs it with the fierce men stirring strife (span-pair): the ambush set within a wider violence. No source is recorded (103 absent) - the crouching menace is presented without cause given. No seat locates it (104 none); manner is unmarked (108 none); intensity, specifier, and effect are unrecorded (109/110/111 absent) - no degree graded, no separate result. Nothing is prohibited (113 absent). The discovery (114) reads it as the predatory ambush, the crouching menace that opens the psalm's alarm. Role is characteristic (115); locus (116) is external:person - oriented on other people. This is a distinct verb from the hope-words, naming the same dark posture: an interior bent on seizing a life, its waiting purely predatory.
narratives.story: The psalm opens in alarm: look, they are lying in ambush for my life. These are violent men crouched and ready, waiting for the moment to seize him. It is a different word from the ones used for hoping in God, but it describes the same posture turned evil - patient watching aimed at destruction. The psalm gives no reason for the hatred; it simply sounds the alarm of a man who knows he is being hunted.
narratives.variation_note: Where the family's hope-verbs describe waiting on God, this arab is a separate verb for predatory ambush; its distinctive is that the waiting is straightforwardly a hunt for a life, opening the psalm in alarm rather than resolving in trust - the dark counterpart, by a different word, to Psa 56:6's inverted qavah.

narratives.narrative: This is the family's keynote of silent waiting: dumiyyah (sense 101: my soul waits in silence) is typed as status (102) - a state of being, not an act. Uniquely, the source is recorded (103): because from God comes his salvation (span-pair) - the silence has a reason. The seat is recorded (104): the soul (span-pair) - here, unusually, the waiting is organ-seated in the nephesh. The bearer (105) is the psalmist, his soul (span-pair). The operation (106) is to wait in silence, to rest quietly, targeted (107) at God alone; and the manner (108) is recorded: in silence, for God alone. The coupling (112) links it to the same posture self-commanded in v5, grounded in hope (span-pair). Intensity, specifier, and effect are unrecorded (109/110/111 absent) - no degree graded, no separate result. Nothing is prohibited (113 absent). The discovery (114) reads it as quiet, exclusive trust - not passive but the deepest active reliance, silence as faith. Role is characteristic (115); locus (116) is external:god. This reading is the richest in the family for recorded dimensions - source, seat, and manner all present - marking silent waiting as a fully specified interior state resting on God alone.
narratives.story: For God alone my soul waits in silence - this is the still centre of the whole psalm. The waiting is not a restless watching but a deep quiet: the soul has stopped its own striving and simply rests on God, from whom rescue will come. And the silence is not empty or passive; it is the most active kind of trust, a stillness that is itself an act of faith. Of all the ways this psalm speaks of waiting, this is the fullest - it tells us where the quiet comes from, that it rises from deep within him, and that it is for God alone. It is a person wholly at rest in God.

narratives.narrative: Here tiqvah 'hope' (sense 101: my hope is from him) is status (type 102) - a settled condition. The seat is recorded (104): the soul (span-pair) - the hope lodged in the nephesh. The bearer (105) is the psalmist. The operation (106) is to hope, to look expectantly, targeted (107) from God - the hope's whole source and direction is God. Manner is recorded (108): waiting in silence (span-pair) - the hope wears the same stillness as v1. No separate source row is given (103 absent) - the ground is carried in 'from him'. Intensity, specifier, and effect are unrecorded (109/110/111 absent) - no degree graded, no separate result. The coupling (112) makes it the ground of the self-commanded silent waiting (span-pair): hope is why the soul can be still. Nothing is prohibited (113 absent). The discovery (114) reads it as the expectation that comes from God alone - the reason the soul can be silent, its whole future in his hand. Role is characteristic (115); locus (116) is external:god. The inner-being movement: the psalmist commands his own soul to be still because its hope is sourced wholly in God.
narratives.story: Now the psalmist turns and tells his own soul to do what the psalm's opening described: for God alone be still, because my hope comes from him. Here hope is the reason the silence is possible - the soul can stop striving precisely because its whole future rests in God's hands. It is a quiet, settled expectation, wearing the same stillness as before, and pointed entirely at God as its source. It is a man grounding his own calm in the fact that everything he hopes for depends on God alone.
narratives.variation_note: This tiqvah differs from Psa 9:18 (the durable hope of the poor as a class) and Psa 71:5 (God named as lifelong hope): here it is the psalmist commanding his own soul, and its distinctive is that hope functions as the ground of silence - the reason the soul can rest - fused to the waiting-in-silence of v1.

narratives.narrative: This is hope at its widest reach: mibtach (sense 101: the hope of all the ends of the earth) is status (type 102) - a confidence, a trust. The source is recorded (103): God of their salvation, who answers with righteousness (span-pair) - the ground of the trust. The bearer (105) is startlingly broad: all the ends of the earth and the farthest seas. The operation (106) is to hope in, to trust, targeted (107) at God; and the manner (108) is recorded: universal, to the farthest seas. But the coupling (112) is explicitly 'none' - no in-verse welding to a further movement, the reading standing alone. No seat locates it (104 none); intensity, specifier, and effect are unrecorded (109/110/111 absent) - no degree graded, no separate result. Nothing is prohibited (113 absent). The discovery (114) reads it as the universal reach of hope in the God who saves - God the confidence of all creation. Role is characteristic (115); locus (116) is external:god. The inner-being lens here widens past the single self to a whole-earth interior: all peoples' trust converging on the one God who answers with righteousness.
narratives.story: This psalm stretches hope to the horizon: God is the confidence of everyone to the ends of the earth and the farthest seas. It is no longer one person's trust but all of creation's, resting on the God who saves and answers with awesome, righteous deeds. The reach is deliberately universal - as far as land and sea go, so far does this hope extend. It is a vision of the whole world's inner life leaning, knowingly or not, on the one God who puts things right.

narratives.narrative: This yachal 'wait/hope' (sense 101: my eyes grow dim with waiting for my God) is action (type 102), waiting worn to exhaustion. The seat is recorded (104): the eyes (inferred) - here the waiting is localised in failing sight. The bearer (105) is the psalmist. The operation (106) is to wait, to hope, targeted (107) at my God; and the manner (108) is recorded: until the eyes grow dim - the strain is carried here, in the physical toll, rather than in a graded intensity row. The coupling (112) pairs it with weary crying (span-pair): waiting welded to exhausted weeping. No source is recorded (103 absent); intensity, specifier, and effect are unrecorded (109/110/111 absent) - the exhaustion is narrated in manner and coupling, not logged as intensity or effect. Nothing is prohibited (113 absent). The discovery (114) reads it as hope stretched to the edge of failing sight - faith at its most exhausted, expectation held even as strength gives out. Role is characteristic (115); locus (116) is external:god. The inner-being movement is hope pushed to its physical limit, the body itself failing while the waiting on God persists.
narratives.story: The psalmist has waited so long and wept so much that his eyes are failing - worn out from watching for a God who has not yet come. Here waiting has a body: it strains the eyes dim and runs alongside weary, throat-parched crying. This is faith at its most exhausted, hope held on even as the strength to hold it drains away. It is the portrait of a person at the very end of his endurance who still keeps looking for God.
narratives.variation_note: Both yachal 'wait' readings fix hope on God, but Psa 38:15 is a deliberate, composed turn from self-defence to trust, whereas this one is hope worn to exhaustion - seated in eyes that fail, coupled to weary weeping. The difference is intensity of strain: resolve there, depletion here.

narratives.narrative: Here qavah 'hope' (sense 101: those who hope in you) is status (type 102), and the reading turns outward toward others. The bearer (105) is those who hope in God - not the psalmist himself but the wider faithful. The operation (106) is to hope in God, targeted (107) at God, and the coupling (112) pairs it with those who seek God (span-pair): the hopers set alongside the seekers. No source is recorded (103 absent); no seat locates it (104 none); manner is unmarked (108 none); intensity, specifier, and effect are unrecorded (109/110/111 absent) - no degree graded, no separate result. Nothing is prohibited (113 absent). The discovery (114) surfaces the striking finding: the psalmist's altruistic dread that his own disgrace might discredit the faithful - his suffering weighed for its effect on others' hope, not just his own. Role is characteristic (115); locus (116) is external:god. The inner-being movement is unusual: the self reckoning its shame against the hope of others, protective of their confidence in God.
narratives.story: In the middle of his own suffering the psalmist worries about other people: don't let those who hope in you be shamed because of me. His fear is not only for himself but that his disgrace might damage the faith of others who are trusting God. Hope here belongs to the wider company of the faithful, set beside those who seek God, and the psalmist guards it as something precious. It is a rare, selfless turn - a suffering man anxious that his trouble not become a reason for anyone else to lose hope.

narratives.narrative: This qavah is hope that reaches for people and finds nothing: 'look/wait for' (sense 101: I looked for pity, but there was none) is action (type 102). The bearer (105) is the psalmist. The operation (106) is to look for, to wait, targeted (107) at pity and comforters - other people, not God. The manner (108) is recorded and devastating: in vain - there was none. The coupling (112) is the loneliness that deepens the despair (span-pair): the failed looking welded to isolation. No source is recorded (103 absent); no seat locates it (104 none); intensity, specifier, and effect are unrecorded (109/110/111 absent) - the emptiness is carried in the manner ('in vain'), not logged as an effect. Nothing is prohibited (113 absent). The discovery (114) reads it as the vain waiting for human sympathy - the utter aloneness that leaves God as the only refuge. Role is characteristic (115); locus (116) is internal:ib-state - the reading is seated in the interior's own desolation rather than on God, because its object (human pity) has failed. The inner-being movement: hope directed at people, met by absence, thrown back on itself.
narratives.story: The psalmist waited for someone - anyone - to show him pity, and no one came; he looked for comforters and found not one. Here the same word used elsewhere for hoping in God is aimed at other people, and it comes back empty. The result is crushing loneliness, the kind that strips away every human support. It is the picture of a person who has reached out for sympathy, found only silence, and is left utterly alone - with God as the only refuge left.

narratives.narrative: This tiqvah 'hope' (sense 101: you, O Lord GOD, are my hope) is status (type 102), and it identifies God himself as the hope. The bearer (105) is the psalmist. The operation (106) is to hope in God, targeted (107) at God - my hope from my youth; and the manner (108) is recorded: from his youth, lifelong. The coupling (112) pairs it with trust from youth (span-pair): hope and trust twinned across a lifetime. No source is recorded (103 absent) beyond God as target; no seat locates it (104 none); intensity, specifier, and effect are unrecorded (109/110/111 absent) - no degree graded, no separate result. Nothing is prohibited (113 absent). The discovery (114) reads it as hope in God spanning a whole life - a confidence not newly found in old age but lifelong, which he begs God not to disappoint. Role is characteristic (115); locus (116) is external:god. The inner-being movement is a hope defined by its duration: God has been the object of this interior's expectation since youth, and now in age it leans on that long history.
narratives.story: Now old, the psalmist looks back over his whole life and says to God: you have been my hope since I was young. This is not a hope discovered late in a crisis but one that has run the length of his years, twinned with a trust he has carried from youth. Because it is so long-standing, it becomes the ground of his plea - do not cast me off now that I am old. It is a person leaning, in old age, on a lifetime of hoping in the same God.
narratives.variation_note: This tiqvah differs from Psa 9:18 (the poor's durable hope as a class) and Psa 62:5 (hope as the ground of silence): here its distinctive is lifelong duration - God named as the psalmist's hope 'from my youth' - making the reading about a whole life's continuity of hope rather than a moment's posture.

narratives.narrative: This yachal 'hope' (sense 101: I will hope continually) is action (type 102) - hope resolved as ongoing act. The source is recorded (103): confident God will revive and comfort him again (span-pair) - the ground of the resolve. The bearer (105) is the psalmist. The operation (106) is to hope, to wait, targeted (107) at God; and the manner (108) is recorded: continually, praising more and more (span-pair). The coupling (112) pairs it with ever-increasing praise (span-pair): hope welded to swelling praise. No seat locates it (104 none); intensity, specifier, and effect are unrecorded (109/110/111 absent) - the 'continually' and 'more and more' sit in manner and coupling rather than a graded intensity row. Nothing is prohibited (113 absent). The discovery (114) reads it as hope renewed against the enemies' scorn - the steady waiting on God that only grows, answering despair with more praise. Role is characteristic (115); locus (116) is external:god. The inner-being movement is hope as a rising trajectory: against mockery, the interior does not merely hold but increases, its hope feeding ever-louder praise.
narratives.story: Surrounded by enemies who want to see him fall, the psalmist plants his flag: but I will keep on hoping, and praise you more and more. His hope is not static - it climbs, and the more he hopes the louder his praise grows. He is sure God will revive and comfort him again, and that confidence is what fuels the rising song. It is a defiant, growing hope that answers scorn not with despair but with ever-increasing worship.
narratives.variation_note: Where other yachal readings show hope as a command to the downcast soul (Psa 42) or hope worn to exhaustion (Psa 69:3), this one is hope on an upward trajectory - 'continually', coupled to praise that grows 'more and more'. Its distinctive is increase: hope that swells against opposition rather than merely holding.

narratives.narrative: This is a rarer hope-word: kesel (sense 101: hope/confidence) is typed as disposition (102) - a settled bent of the inner life. The bearer (105) is the children - the next generation being taught. The operation (106) is to set one's hope, targeted (107) at God, and the coupling (112) pairs it with not forgetting and keeping God's works (v7): hope welded to memory and obedience. No source is recorded (103 absent); no seat locates it (104 none); manner is unmarked (108 none); intensity, specifier, and effect are unrecorded (109/110/111 absent) - no degree graded, no separate result. Nothing is prohibited (113 absent). The discovery (114) reads it as the whole aim of transmission: confidence fixed on God rather than self. Role is characteristic (115); locus (116) is external:god. The inner-being movement here is generational: the point of passing on God's deeds is to shape, in children yet unborn, an interior disposed to set its hope on God - hope as the intended outcome of teaching, bound up with remembering and obeying.
narratives.story: The whole reason for telling the next generation what God has done is spelled out here: so that the children will grow up to put their hope in God. This hope is a settled leaning of the heart, and it comes bundled with two companions - not forgetting God's works, and keeping his commands. The aim is to shape young lives whose confidence rests on God rather than on themselves. It is hope as something deliberately handed down, meant to take root in children not yet born.

narratives.narrative: This reading is a failure of waiting, and must be read with equal weight to the faithful ones. chakah 'wait' (sense 101) appears negated - they did NOT wait - typed as disposition (102). The bearer (105) is the fathers, the wilderness generation. The operation (106) is to fail to wait, targeted (107) at God's counsel: they would not wait for it. The coupling (112) is external:god - the failure is over against God. No source is recorded (103 absent); no seat locates it (104 none); manner is unmarked (108 none); intensity, specifier, and effect are unrecorded (109/110/111 absent) - no degree graded, no separate result. Nothing is prohibited (113 absent) as a row, though the whole reading is the breach of what waiting requires. The discovery (114) reads it as the impatience that would not trust God's timing. Role is characteristic (115); and the locus (116) is telling: 'paired with forgetting' - the not-waiting is bound to the forgetting of God's works. The inner-being movement is the negative image of the whole family: an interior that will not hold still for God, its impatience welded to forgetfulness.
narratives.story: Here the psalm shows what happens when waiting collapses: the fathers in the wilderness did not wait for God's counsel - they soon forgot what he had done and rushed ahead of him. This is the exact opposite of hopeful waiting: an impatience that refuses to trust God's timing, tied hand-in-hand with forgetting his works. The psalm does not soften it. It is the dark mirror of every faithful wait in these psalms - a people who could not hold still for God, and paid for it.

narratives.narrative: This yachal/sabar 'hope' (sense 101) is disposition (type 102): the settled bent of hope threaded through Psalm 119. The bearer (105) is the psalmist. The operation (106) is to hope, to wait, targeted (107) at God's word - here, distinctively for the psalm, the object of hope is the word, God's rules. The coupling (112) binds it to the whole hope-arc of the psalm: this is one node in a repeated interior posture. No source is recorded (103 absent); no seat locates it (104 none); manner is unmarked (108 none); intensity, specifier, and effect are unrecorded (109/110/111 absent) - no degree graded, no separate result. Nothing is prohibited (113 absent). The discovery (114) reads it as hope resting in God's rules. Role is characteristic (115); locus (116) is external:god. This reading recurs at four further points in the psalm (v49, v81, v114, v147) - the same disposition surfacing again and again. The inner-being movement is hope given a concrete foothold: not free-floating expectancy but expectation anchored to God's spoken word.
narratives.story: Right through this long psalm the writer keeps coming back to one thing: his hope is in God's word. Even when begging that the truth not be taken from his mouth, he holds fast to it - my hope is in your rules. Hope here is a steady habit of the heart, and what makes it distinctive is where it rests: not on vague expectation but on the concrete promises God has spoken, and he keeps steadying himself there. The same note sounds again and again across the psalm. It is a person who has tied his whole future to the reliability of what God has said.
narratives.variation_note: Across Psalm 119 the same hope-disposition recurs, and this anchor stands for them all; its defining mark, setting it apart from hope aimed simply at God (as in Psa 42 or 130:7), is that the object of hope is specifically God's word - his rules and promises - the foothold that steadies the waiting.

narratives.narrative: This yachal/sabar 'hope' (sense 101: I have hoped in your word) is disposition (type 102), and it is registered under a distinct char-key as the completed 'hoped' - hope already exercised. The bearer (105) is the psalmist. The operation (106) is to hope, to wait, targeted (107) at God's word, and the coupling (112) binds it to the psalm's whole hope-arc. No source is recorded (103 absent); no seat locates it (104 none); manner is unmarked (108 none); intensity, specifier, and effect are unrecorded (109/110/111 absent) - no degree graded, no separate result. Nothing is prohibited (113 absent). The discovery (114) surfaces the distinctive finding: hope that gladdens the God-fearing who witness it - 'those who fear you shall see me and rejoice, because I have hoped in your word.' Role is characteristic (115); locus (116) is external:god. The inner-being movement here is hope that has become visible and contagious: the psalmist's settled expectancy in God's word is not private but seen by others, and its being seen produces joy in the God-fearing. Hope in one interior becomes encouragement to another.
narratives.story: The psalmist pictures other believers catching sight of him and being glad - and the reason for their joy is that he has staked everything on God's word. His hope here is something he has already lived out, and it has become visible: those who fear God see it and rejoice. Hope in one person's heart turns into encouragement for others. It is the picture of a life whose trust in God's promises quietly gladdens everyone who watches it.

narratives.narrative: This qavah is the wicked's ambush inside Psalm 119: 'lie in wait' (sense 101) is action (type 102), bearer (105) the wicked. The operation (106) is to lie in wait, targeted (107) at the psalmist - they wait to destroy him. The coupling (112) sets it within its char-arc across the psalm. No source is recorded (103 absent); no seat locates it (104 none); manner is unmarked (108 none); intensity, specifier, and effect are unrecorded (109/110/111 absent) - no degree graded, no separate result. Nothing is prohibited (113 absent). The discovery (114) reads it as the ambush of the wicked, met by pondering the word: 'the wicked lie in wait to destroy me, but I ponder your testimonies.' Role is characteristic (115); locus (116) is external:person. Read with full weight: the same verb the psalm elsewhere uses for hoping in God is here the wicked's patient lurking - hope inverted into a wait for destruction. The finding is the contrast the verse itself draws: predatory waiting on one side, the interior steadied by meditation on the other.
narratives.story: Even in this psalm of devotion to God's word, the enemy appears: the wicked are lying in wait to destroy the writer. It is the same word used elsewhere for patiently hoping in God, here turned into a patient hope for his ruin. But the verse sets a striking answer beside the threat - while they lurk, he quietly ponders God's teachings. It is a portrait of menace met not by panic but by meditation: their dark waiting against his settled attention to God's word.
narratives.variation_note: Among these qavah readings this is one of the dark ones - the wicked's ambush rather than a worshipper's hope; its distinctive is the deliberate contrast the verse draws, the predatory waiting answered by the psalmist pondering God's testimonies, so the inverted hope is set directly against faithful attention.

narratives.narrative: This seber/sabar 'hope' (sense 101) is disposition (type 102), and it appears at a point of fear: let me not be put to shame in my hope. The bearer (105) is the psalmist. The operation (106) is to hope, to wait, targeted (107) at God's word, and the coupling (112) binds it to the psalm's whole hope-arc. No source is recorded (103 absent); no seat locates it (104 none); manner is unmarked (108 none); intensity, specifier, and effect are unrecorded (109/110/111 absent) - no degree graded, no separate result. Nothing is prohibited (113 absent). The discovery (114) reads it as the hope that must not be shamed - 'uphold me according to your promise, that I may live, and let me not be put to shame in my hope.' Role is characteristic (115); locus (116) is external:god. The inner-being movement is hope conscious of its own vulnerability: the psalmist knows that hope staked on God's promise can, in principle, be disappointed, and he pleads that his not be. Hope here leans on God's promise and asks that promise to hold it up.
narratives.story: Here hope shows its tender underside: the psalmist begs God to hold him up as he promised, so that he may live and not be shamed in the hope he has placed in him. He knows that to hope is to risk disappointment, and he pleads that his hope in God's word not be the thing that fails him. Hope here rests entirely on God's promise and asks that promise to bear its weight. It is a person aware that everything he is counting on depends on God keeping his word.
narratives.variation_note: Both seber/sabar 'hope' readings rest on God, but this one (Psa 119:116) is hope conscious of its risk - pleading not to be shamed - whereas at Psa 146:5 the same word names the settled blessedness of the one whose hope is rightly placed. The difference is posture: vulnerability and petition here, beatitude and security there.

narratives.narrative: This sabar 'hope' (sense 101: I hope for your salvation) is disposition (type 102). The bearer (105) is the psalmist. The operation (106) is to hope, to wait, targeted (107) at God's word - and specifically, in the verse, at God's salvation. The coupling (112) binds it to the psalm's whole hope-arc, and the verse itself couples it to obedience: 'I hope for your salvation, O LORD, and I do your commandments.' No source is recorded (103 absent); no seat locates it (104 none); manner is unmarked (108 none); intensity, specifier, and effect are unrecorded (109/110/111 absent) - no degree graded, no separate result. Nothing is prohibited (113 absent). The discovery (114) reads it as hope for salvation joined to obedience. Role is characteristic (115); locus (116) is external:god. The inner-being movement is hope that does not wait idly: expectation of God's salvation runs in the same breath as active keeping of his commandments - looking for rescue while living obediently.
narratives.story: Near the end of the long psalm the writer says plainly: I am waiting for your salvation, LORD - and in the same breath, and I keep your commandments. His hope for rescue does not make him passive; it runs alongside obedient living. Looking to God to save and doing what God asks are, for him, one life. It is the picture of a person who waits for deliverance not with folded hands but with a life still bent to God's will.

narratives.narrative: In Psalm 130 the hope-words cluster densely; this yachal 'hope' (sense 101) is disposition (type 102), bearer (105) the psalmist. The operation (106) is to hope, targeted (107) at God's word - 'and in his word I hope.' The coupling (112) is external:god, and the locus (116) is 'paired with the waiting' - this hope is explicitly welded to the qavah waiting of the same verse. No source is recorded (103 absent); no seat locates it (104 none); manner is unmarked (108 none); intensity, specifier, and effect are unrecorded (109/110/111 absent) - no degree graded, no separate result. Nothing is prohibited (113 absent). The discovery (114) reads it as the waiting given a foothold in the word - expectation resting on a promise. Role is characteristic (115). The inner-being movement is the crucial hinge of the verse: the naked waiting on the LORD is anchored by hoping in his word, so that the two verbs together make one grounded posture - the self stretched toward God, but stretched onto a promise.
narratives.story: In this psalm the writer waits for the LORD and, in the very same line, hopes in his word - and the two belong together. The waiting would be bare on its own; hoping in God's promise gives it something firm to hold onto. So his expectation is not left hanging in the air but rests on what God has said. It is a person reaching out toward God with his whole self, but reaching onto the solid ground of a promise.
narratives.variation_note: This yachal 'hope' is one of several hope/wait verbs stacked in Psa 130:5-7; its distinctive against the qavah 'wait' of the same verse is that it names the object - God's word - giving the waiting its foothold, and against the corporate hope of v7 it is the psalmist's own. It is the grounding term in the verse's cluster.

narratives.narrative: This qavah 'wait' (sense 101) in Psalm 130 is action (type 102), bearer (105) the psalmist. The operation (106) is simply to wait, targeted (107) at the LORD - 'I wait for the LORD.' The coupling (112) is external:god, and the locus (116) is 'paired with the soul's waiting and hope' - this waiting sits inside a dense cluster of hope-verbs. No source is recorded (103 absent); no seat locates it (104 none); manner is unmarked (108 none); intensity, specifier, and effect are unrecorded (109/110/111 absent) - no degree graded, no separate result. Nothing is prohibited (113 absent). The discovery (114) reads it as expectant waiting: the whole self stretched forward toward God. Role is characteristic (115). The inner-being movement is waiting in its barest, most concentrated form - the self simply leaning toward God - which the surrounding verbs (the soul's waiting, the hoping in the word) then deepen and ground. Held as a distinct row because the verb recurs within the verse.
narratives.story: Out of the depths the psalmist says it as plainly as it can be said: I wait for the LORD. This is waiting stripped to its essence - the whole self leaning forward toward God with nothing else in view. In the lines around it the same longing is repeated and tied down to God's word, but here it stands bare and concentrated. It is the simplest possible posture of a soul out of its depths: just waiting, wholly turned toward God.
narratives.variation_note: Psa 130:5 stacks the wait-verb more than once; this reading is the first, barest statement - 'I wait for the LORD' - distinct from its twin (#11) which doubles and grounds the waiting in the soul and the word. The difference is concentration: here the naked act, there the act deepened.

narratives.narrative: This second qavah 'wait' (sense 101) in Psalm 130 is action (type 102), bearer (105) the psalmist, but now doubled and grounded: 'my soul waits, and in his word I hope.' The operation (106) is to wait, targeted (107) at the LORD, hoping in his word - the target already reaching toward the word. The coupling (112) is external:god, and the locus (116) is 'paired with the soul and hope' - the waiting bound to both the nephesh and the hoping. No source is recorded (103 absent); no seat locates it (104 none) - though the verse names the soul, this row does not seat the waiting in an organ; manner is unmarked (108 none); intensity, specifier, and effect are unrecorded (109/110/111 absent) - no degree graded, no separate result. Nothing is prohibited (113 absent). The discovery (114) reads it as the waiting doubled and grounded - expectation anchored in God's word. Role is characteristic (115). The inner-being movement is the intensification of #10: the bare waiting is now the soul's whole waiting, and it is fastened to the word. The repetition itself is the finding - waiting said twice, deepened each time.
narratives.story: The psalmist says it again, and this time fuller: my soul waits - my whole inner self - and I put my hope in his word. The simple waiting of the line before is now deepened into the longing of his whole soul, and it is tied down to God's promise. Saying it twice, and grounding it the second time, is the point: this is waiting pressed deeper and given something solid to rest on. It is a soul that waits with everything it has, holding onto what God has said.
narratives.variation_note: This is the doubled, grounded form of the wait-verb in Psa 130:5, distinct from its bare twin (#10): here the waiting is the soul's whole waiting and is anchored to God's word. The repetition and deepening are themselves the finding - the same act intensified within a single verse.

narratives.narrative: This yachal 'hope' (sense 101) in Psalm 130 is disposition (type 102), but the bearer (105) widens from the psalmist to Israel - 'O Israel, hope in the LORD!' The operation (106) is to hope, targeted (107) at the LORD, and the coupling (112) is external:god. The locus (116) is 'paired with God's steadfast love and redemption' - the call to hope grounded in what follows: 'for with the LORD there is steadfast love, and with him is plentiful redemption.' No separate source row is given (103 absent); no seat locates it (104 none); manner is unmarked (108 none); intensity, specifier, and effect are unrecorded (109/110/111 absent) - no degree graded, no separate result. Nothing is prohibited (113 absent). The discovery (114) reads it as the hope widened from the self to the whole people, grounded in God's plentiful redemption. Role is characteristic (115); its orientation is toward God. The inner-being movement is the turn outward: the individual's hard-won hope becomes a summons to the whole community, and it is grounded not in the people's worthiness but in God's steadfast love and abundant redemption.
narratives.story: Having found hope for himself out of the depths, the psalmist turns and calls the whole nation to the same thing: Israel, hope in the LORD! And he gives the reason - with the LORD there is faithful love and more than enough redemption. The hope one person discovered becomes a summons to everyone, resting not on how good the people are but on how generous God is. It is a man who has been rescued from the pit urging his whole people to hope in the God who rescued him.
narratives.variation_note: Where the earlier Psa 130 hope (v5) is the psalmist's own, personal and word-anchored, this reading widens the bearer to all Israel and grounds the call in God's steadfast love and plentiful redemption. The distinctive is the turn from private hope to a corporate summons.

narratives.narrative: This yachal 'hope' (sense 101) closes Psalm 131 as disposition (type 102), bearer (105) Israel - 'O Israel, hope in the LORD from this time forth and forevermore.' The operation (106) is to hope, targeted (107) at the LORD, coupling (112) external:god. The locus (116) is 'paired with the stilled soul' - the call to hope grows directly out of the preceding image of a soul quieted like a weaned child. No separate source row is given (103 absent); no seat locates it (104 none); manner is unmarked (108 none); intensity, specifier, and effect are unrecorded (109/110/111 absent) - no degree graded, no separate result. Nothing is prohibited (113 absent). The discovery (114) reads it as the stilled trust widened to the whole people - hope as the settled posture, from now and forever. Role is characteristic (115). The inner-being movement is the outward turn of a quieted heart: having calmed and stilled his own soul like a weaned child, the psalmist calls Israel into the same settled, unhurried hope, extended across all time.
narratives.story: The little psalm of a quieted heart ends by inviting everyone in: Israel, hope in the LORD, now and for all time. Just before, the writer described his soul as calmed and settled, like a weaned child resting against its mother. Now he turns that stilled contentment into a call for the whole people to hope the same way. It is a quiet, unhurried hope stretched out over all time - the peace of one settled heart offered to a nation.
narratives.variation_note: This yachal call parallels the corporate summons at Psa 130:7, but its distinctive ground is the stilled soul of Psa 131:2 - hope here flows from a heart already quieted like a weaned child, and it is stretched 'from this time forth and forevermore', making it the settled, timeless posture rather than a rescue-born plea.

narratives.narrative: This seber/sabar 'hope' (sense 101: hope in the God of Jacob) is affect (type 102), set inside a beatitude. The bearer (105) is the blessed - 'blessed is he whose help and hope is in the God of Jacob.' The operation (106) is the beatitude itself: blessed is the one whose help and hope is in the God of Jacob - hope rightly placed - targeted (107) at rightly-placed-hope. The coupling (112) hope-in-God binds the interior movement to its right object. No source is recorded (103 absent); no seat locates it (104 none); manner is unmarked (108 none); intensity, specifier, and effect are unrecorded (109/110/111 absent) - no degree graded, no separate result. Nothing is prohibited (113 absent). The discovery (114) reads it against the perishing plans of princes: where human help fails at death, the interior fastens its hope on the maker who keeps faith forever. Role is characteristic (115); locus (116) is internal:ib-state - the reading is seated in the blessed interior's own condition, with the God of Jacob as the object it rests on. The inner-being movement is hope defined by the rightness of its object: happiness itself consists in hoping in the right God rather than in mortal princes whose plans die with them.
narratives.story: The psalm pronounces a blessing: how happy is the person whose help and hope rest on the God of Jacob. It sets this against trusting human leaders, whose breath departs and whose plans die with them the same day. Real, lasting happiness, it says, belongs to the one who fastens hope on the God who made everything and keeps faith forever. Hope here is measured by its object - and the whole point is that hoping in the right God is itself a kind of blessedness.
narratives.variation_note: Both seber/sabar 'hope' readings rest on God, but this Psa 146:5 instance frames hope as beatitude - the settled blessedness of the rightly-placed hope, set against perishing human help - whereas Psa 119:116 is hope conscious of its risk, pleading not to be shamed. Security and blessing here; vulnerability and petition there.

narratives.narrative: This yachal 'hope' (sense 101: hope in steadfast love) closes the family as affect (type 102). The bearer (105) is those who hope. The operation (106) is the hope set on God's steadfast love, paired with fear as what pleases God - 'the LORD takes pleasure in those who fear him, in those who hope in his steadfast love' - targeted (107) at steadfast-hope. The coupling (112) hope-in-chesed binds the interior movement to covenant love as its resting-place. No source is recorded (103 absent); no seat locates it (104 none); manner is unmarked (108 none); intensity, specifier, and effect are unrecorded (109/110/111 absent) - no degree graded, no separate result. Nothing is prohibited (113 absent). The discovery (114) reads it distinct from fear: hope leans forward onto covenant love where fear looks up in reverence - and the two together are what God delights in. Role is characteristic (115); locus (116) is internal:ib-state - seated in the interior's own condition, oriented toward God's steadfast love. The inner-being movement is hope as the object of God's own pleasure: not the fearsome strength of the horse or the runner's legs, but the interior that leans on God's love, is what delights him.
narratives.story: The psalm says something surprising about what pleases God: not the strength of a warhorse or the speed of a runner, but people who fear him and put their hope in his faithful love. Hope here is a leaning-forward of the heart onto God's steady, covenant love, and it stands side by side with reverent awe. Where awe looks up, hope leans in - and God takes delight in exactly this. It is the picture of an inner life that trusts God's love, and finds that this very trust is what gladdens him.
narratives.variation_note: This yachal closes the family echoing Psa 33:18's pairing of hope with fear and its resting on God's steadfast love; the distinctive here is that hope is named as the object of God's own pleasure - set against the strength of horse and runner - so the reading frames rightly-placed hope as what delights God, not merely what he watches over.
